newsitem.title: UK: Britain releases BCCI fraudster wanted by U.S..
newsitem.headline: Britain releases BCCI fraudster wanted by U.S..

text.p: Britain's High Court on Wednesday released a key figure in the world's biggest banking fraud from prison, saying he had been waiting too long for his extradition to the United States.

Lord Justice Sir Christopher Rose and Justice Maurice Kay gave the United States 24 hours from Tuesday to appeal against their decision to release Syed Ziauddin Ali Akbar, former treasury head at the Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI).
The United States wanted to try Ali Akbar, who has dual British-Pakistani nationalityu, on blackmail charges. But Washington's lawyers in London said they had decided not to appeal.

Ali Akbar, 50, was sentenced to six years imprisonment in Britain in 1993 for his part in the $12 billion collapse of BCCI, after the Luxembourg-based bank was found to be operating a global money-laundering network.
He was released in August 1995, but re-arrested immediately at the request of the United States and had been awaiting extradition in a south London prison since then.
Under British law, anyone being held for extradition may appeal for release after two months.
The United States has blamed the delay on a disagreement between Britain and France, which is objecting to Ali Akbar's extradition.

"The Justice Dept has taken every step possible to ensure Mr. Akbar's extradition, but for the last year we've been forced to wait, hoping that Britain and France could resolve problems identified by the British courts," said a Justice Department spokesman in Washington.
The problem arose because the former BBCI treasurer fled to France in 1991 while on parole in Britain for a drug trafficking offence.
Paris agreed to extradite him to Britain to face trial for money laundering but is now opposed to his re-extradition to the U.S. to face a different set of charges.
Britain's Home Office (interior ministry) said it was up to Washington to sort out the problem.
The collapse of BCCI left a quarter of a million creditors stranded around the world and shook the regulatory authorities that were accused of failing to spot its illegal activities.
The bank had assets of $24 billion and operations in 71 countries when it was shut down.
